title: Continents that fit
teaches: Wegener's evidence that the continents have moved, and why most geologists rejected it for forty years

blocks.text: Almost anyone who looks at a world map notices that the bulge of Brazil would tuck into the curve of West Africa. The Flemish mapmaker Abraham Ortelius remarked on it as early as 1596, suggesting that the Americas had been torn away from Europe and Africa by earthquakes and floods. For three centuries the observation remained little more than a geographical curiosity.

In January 1912 a German meteorologist named Alfred Wegener gave a lecture in Frankfurt arguing that the fit was a clue to the history of the Earth. He proposed that all the continents had once been joined in a single landmass, which he later called **Pangaea** ("all land"), and that it had broken apart, the pieces drifting to their present positions. He set out the case at length in 1915 in a book, *The Origin of Continents and Oceans*, and kept revising and expanding it until his death.

Wegener recognized that a coastline is a poor place to look for the true edge of a continent. Around most land, the sea floor slopes gently out to a depth of a hundred metres or so before dropping off toward the deep ocean floor, three to five kilometres down. The gently sloping rim, the **continental shelf**, is simply part of the continent that happens to be flooded; when sea level fell during the ice ages, much of it was dry land. If continents had split apart, the edges that ought to match are the steep drop-offs beyond the shelves, regardless of where the shoreline happens to stand today.

blocks.caption: South America and Africa, shown by their coastlines or by the steep drop beyond their continental shelves (the 1,000 m depth line). Closing the ocean swings South America about a single fixed point on the globe near the Azores, the way a door swings on its hinge.
blocks.task: Close the Atlantic using the shelf edges

blocks.text: Wegener could only work with maps and globe measurements. A rigorous geometric test came in 1965, when Edward Bullard, Jim Everett and Alan Smith at Cambridge used an early computer to find the closest fit of the continents around the Atlantic along the 500-fathom contour (a fathom is six feet, so about 900 m down, partway down the steep drop beyond the shelf). The figure uses their rotation, drawn at the nearby 1,000 m depth line. Along most of the join, the gaps and overlaps are under a hundred kilometres, and the largest overlap is the Niger delta, a pile of sediment built out by the river long after the continents separated.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Wegener proposed that the continents were once joined in a single landmass, Pangaea, which later broke apart.
The continental shelf is flooded continental rock, so the drop-off beyond the shelf marks a continent's true outline better than the shoreline.
South America and Africa fit within about a hundred kilometres along the steep slopes beyond their shelves.

blocks.text: A good geometric fit could still be coincidence. Wegener's stronger argument was that the rocks and fossils match right across the join, as if a torn sheet of newspaper could be put back together by the shapes of its ragged edges and then checked by reading the lines of print across the tear.

Fossils of **Mesosaurus**, a slender reptile about a metre long that lived in fresh or brackish water some 280 million years ago, are known only from southern Brazil, Uruguay and southern Africa. An animal built for shallow inland waters could not have swum the South Atlantic. Leaves of **Glossopteris**, a seed-bearing tree whose heavy seeds were ill-suited to blowing or floating across oceans, turn up in rocks of similar age across South America, Africa, India, Antarctica and Australia.

blocks.caption: A fossil Mesosaurus from the Paraná Basin in Brazil. Skeletons like this one also turn up in southern Africa.
South America fitted against Africa along the 1,000 m depth line, with Mesosaurus fossils and two-billion-year-old rocks matching across the join.
A Glossopteris leaf from Antarctica, with its strong central vein. The same kind of leaf is found in South America, Africa, India and Australia.

blocks.text: Geological structures match across the water in the same way. A belt of folded mountains about 250 million years old, the Cape Fold Belt of South Africa, lines up with the Sierra de la Ventana in Argentina when the Atlantic is closed. Decades after Wegener's death, radiometric dating showed that a small patch of two-billion-year-old rock near São Luís on the coast of Brazil is a direct continuation of an equally ancient rock province in Ghana, with a sharp boundary against younger rocks that lines up across the ocean.

Some of the strongest evidence came from ancient ice. In South Africa, India, Australia and South America (and, discovered later, Antarctica) there are beds of **tillite**, a rock formed from hardened glacial debris: boulders of many kinds set in a fine, ground-up matrix, resting on bedrock scratched and polished by moving ice (the subject of lesson 13). These beds are about 300 million years old, and many now lie in the tropics. On a modern map the bedrock scratches point in directions that make no sense, in several places showing ice creeping inland from what is now open ocean. Gather the southern continents together around southern Africa and Antarctica, and the scratches radiate outward from a single polar ice sheet, like spokes from a hub. For this southern supercontinent, which formed the southern half of Pangaea, Wegener used the name **Gondwana**, coined in 1885 by the Austrian geologist Eduard Suess.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Freshwater and land fossils such as Mesosaurus and Glossopteris occur on continents now separated by wide oceans.
Mountain belts, ancient rock provinces and 300-million-year-old glacial deposits align when the continents are reassembled.
The southern continents together formed Gondwana, the southern portion of Pangaea.

blocks.text: Most geologists, particularly in Britain and North America, rejected continental drift, sometimes with open scorn. At a symposium held by petroleum geologists in New York in 1926, speaker after speaker dismantled the theory. Part of their hostility was territorial, aimed at a meteorologist who presumed to tell geologists how to read their own rocks. Yet the central objection was entirely reasonable: Wegener had no credible physics to move a continent.

He pointed to two possible driving forces: a slight tendency for buoyant continents to creep toward the equator on a spinning, slightly flattened Earth, and the westward drag of tidal attraction from the Sun and Moon. In 1924 the Cambridge geophysicist Harold Jeffreys calculated that both forces were millions of times too weak to shift a continent. Worse still, Wegener pictured the granitic continents ploughing through the denser rock of the ocean floor like icebreakers through pack ice. Jeffreys showed that the floor of the ocean is far too rigid for that; a continent pushed against it would crumple rather than cut a path.

To account for identical fossils on opposite sides of the oceans, orthodox geologists relied on narrow land bridges that had supposedly linked the continents and laterfoundered into the abyss. That explanation, however, ran straight into the principle of buoyancy covered in lesson 5. Continental crust is less dense than the mantle rock beneath it and floats on it like a loaded barge. A broad strip of continent can no more sink to the floor of the deep ocean than a plank of wood can sink to the bottom of a pond. Geologists who dismissed Wegener on physical grounds were defending sunken land bridges that violated the very same physics.

Wegener kept gathering evidence. In November 1930, during his fourth expedition to the Greenland ice sheet, he died shortly after his fiftieth birthday while returning on skis from resupplying an isolated weather station on the central ice. His hypothesis stayed alive among a small minority of geologists. In South Africa, where the glacial beds and Glossopteris fossils were underfoot, Alexander du Toit mapped the matching geology of the southern continents in detail; in Britain, Arthur Holmes proposed between 1928 and 1931 that slow convection currents in the hot mantle beneath the crust could carry the continents on their backs. Holmes had hit on the right kind of engine, though with no way to observe the mantle or the ocean floor, the idea gained little traction.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Continental drift was rejected chiefly because the forces Wegener proposed were millions of times too weak, and continents cannot plough through rigid ocean floor.
The orthodox alternative, sunken land bridges, contradicted the buoyancy of continental crust.
Arthur Holmes suggested by 1931 that slow convection currents in the mantle could carry the continents.

blocks.text: Both camps had argued almost entirely from the geology of dry land, which covers less than a third of the globe. Hardly anyone knew what kind of rock floored the deep oceans, how old it was, or even the shape of its topography beyond sparse lines of lead-line and early echo-sounder measurements. That ignorance ended after the Second World War, when navies began charting the sea bed in detail to hide and hunt submarines, and discovered a landscape unlike anything predicted.

Winding down the middle of the Atlantic is a continuous submarine mountain range, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, mirroring the curve of the continental margins on either side. Along its high crest runs a steep-walled rift valley, and shallow earthquakes trace that valley like a string of beads. The next lesson follows the clue that explained what was happening there, preserved in the magnetism of the basalt on the ocean floor.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: The evidence that resolved the debate over continental drift lay on the ocean floor, which remained largely unmapped until after 1945.

blocks.caption: Five questions on continental drift
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: Why do South America and Africa fit more closely along the 1,000 m depth line than along their present coastlines?
choices: The continental shelf is flooded continent, so the steep drop beyond it marks the true edge of the continental crust
Ocean waves have eroded both coastlines back by hundreds of kilometres since the split
The continental shelves were built out of volcanic rock after the Atlantic opened
items.why: Where the shoreline sits depends on current sea level. The steep slope beyond the shallow shelf marks where buoyant continental crust gives way to the deep ocean basin.

items.ask: What makes Mesosaurus a strong piece of evidence that South America and Africa were once joined?
choices: It was a small reptile adapted to fresh or brackish water, incapable of swimming across the South Atlantic
It was a wide-ranging marine reptile whose fossils occur in every ocean basin
It lived recently enough that human observers recorded the split of its habitat
items.why: A metre-long reptile confined to shallow inland waters could not cross several thousand kilometres of open ocean, yet its fossils appear on both sides of the South Atlantic and nowhere else.

items.ask: In southern Africa, India and Australia, 300-million-year-old glacial scratches on bedrock point in directions that look nonsensical today, sometimes running inland from the sea. How does continental drift account for this?
choices: When the southern continents are reassembled into Gondwana, the scratches radiate outward from a single polar ice sheet
The weight of the ice depressed the continents so that glaciers flowed uphill from the ocean
The entire Earth was encased in ice at the time, so glaciers moved in random directions
items.why: Reassembling the southern landmasses around southern Africa and Antarctica brings the glaciated regions together near the pole, with the ice-flow directions pointing outward from one centre.

items.ask: What was the strongest scientific objection raised against Wegener's theory in the 1920s?
choices: The driving forces he proposed were millions of times too weak, and continents would crumple if pushed through rigid ocean floor
Computer reconstructions showed that the continental shelves overlapped by more than a thousand kilometres
Radiometric dating proved that the matching rock belts on opposite sides of the Atlantic had different ages
items.why: Harold Jeffreys demonstrated that tidal drag and equatorial drift were far too feeble to move continents, and that oceanic rock was too strong for continents to plough through it.

items.ask: Why did the rival idea of sunken land bridges fail on physical grounds?
choices: Low-density continental crust floats on the denser mantle and cannot sink to the floor of the deep ocean
Land bridges narrow enough to sink would have been too steep for land plants like Glossopteris to cross
Sinking so much land would have lowered global sea level rather than drowning the bridges
items.why: Because continental crust is much more buoyant than the mantle beneath it, a continental land bridge cannot simply founder into the deep ocean floor.

learned: Wegener proposed that the continents were once joined in a single supercontinent, Pangaea, and later drifted apart.
South America and Africa fit closely along the steep slopes beyond their continental shelves, and fossils, mountain belts and ancient glacial beds match across the join.
Continental drift was rejected for decades because Wegener had no workable physical mechanism to move continents.
The decisive evidence eventually came from mapping and sampling the deep ocean floor after 1945.
